Being a founder is like "chewing glass"

"When you spend six months recruiting a candidate and they don't join, that's chewing glass. 

When you spend a bunch of time working on a product that gets completely washed over by the next model and makes you feel like an idiot for expending all that time and capacity on something that was the wrong call, chewing glass. 

When you get rejected by 40 investors in a row before you're able to raise capital, chewing glass.

My experience of startup building is it's like a rollercoaster where you have to feel the extreme highs and feel the extreme lows, and I'm a super emotional guy. 

I will feel on top of the world at the high and like everything is cataclysmic at the low.

But then if I look back at the journey, the lows get lower, the highs get much higher. 

And I look back three months ago at the low I was dealing with, I was like, 'What a joke.' I could do that in my sleep now."

Bitcoin is pumping, but US spot demand still isn’t confirming the move.

The Coinbase Premium is back below 0, meaning BTC trades slightly cheaper on Coinbase than on Binance.

That doesn’t guarantee a retrace, but without stronger spot buying, the rally could be easier for perp traders to fade.

IMO, 3 things need to happen:

1. The Coinbase Premium needs to reclaim zero.
2. It needs to remain positive, not just briefly cross above it.
3. Ideally, it should rise alongside BTC, showing that Coinbase buyers are supporting the move.

The rally can continue without this, but a sustained positive premium would make it much more convincing.

For now, I’m watching to see whether US spot demand catches up with the price.

This year's All-In Summit brought together builders, researchers, and policymakers shaping the future of AI, energy, and markets.

I asked Satya “where’s the magic?”, and his main insight was as simple as it was smart: most people's lived experience hasn’t been improved by AI yet. But the mistake that had the biggest effect on me was in 1982. I had calculated that American banks had lent a lot of money to a bunch of countries that would not be able to pay it back. Mexico defaulted in August 1982, and while I was right about that part, I was completely wrong about the market. I thought the stock market was going to go down, but it went up because the Federal Reserve eased.

I didn't just miss. I was publicly wrong and lost everything. I lost my company and all the people who worked for me—people who were like family. I was the only one left. I had to borrow $4,000 from my dad just to help pay my family bills.

It was one of the most painful experiences I have ever had, but it was also one of the best. It completely changed my attitude about decision-making. It taught me to move from thinking "I'm right" to asking myself, "How do I know I'm right?"
